items.title: Jimmy Owens — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So, when I quit, the first gig I got was with Slide Hampton and his octet.

ctx.x: So, after you left high school and you spent that time practicing, then what happened?

Well, like I said, I told my boss that I was going to quit and make more money in one night than I made in a whole two weeks. So, when I quit, the first gig I got was with Slide Hampton and his octet. We went to North Carolina to play a concert. I got paid $300 for the concert, okay?

items.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jimmy Owens was one of the people that was organizing that. He asked me to join it as musical director

ctx.x: One association that I’ve neglected to ask you about, that I wanted to ask you about, is the Collective Black Artists, that organization – what your role was in that, what they were about.

When I finally came back to America, one of the things that encouraged me to stay was things like the Collective Black Artists, which was subsidized by the government. Jimmy Owens was one of the people that was organizing that. He asked me to join it as musical director, where I would be conducting things, and writing – composing things and writing arrangements for other people’s compositions. I wrote – I did some things for Jackie McLean, when I first worked with that organization. I’m very sorry to say that…
What was its duration? How long – what was the life of that organization?

items.title: Slide Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, West Orange, New Jersey, July 30, 2003
items.q: That orchestra I think Jimmy Owens had a great deal to do with that orchestra. And I got to write quite a few things for them.

ctx.x: Oh gosh. I didn’t ask you about the Black Artists’ Orchestra, the Manhattan Composers’ Orchestra.

Oh yeah. That orchestra I think Jimmy Owens had a great deal to do with that orchestra. And I got to write quite a few things for them. It was a wonderful experience because I was free to do whatever I wanted to, usually some kind of direction in the program, but it was a chance to have the freedom as far as the things that I wanted to try, the things that I wanted to experiment with and all of that. It was a wonderful opportunity for me so I think I had a chance to do a lot of good things there, to learn a lot…
What did you think of the — I guess they would have called it the avante garde period, free jazz and so forth, that Ornette was doing and some of Coltrane’s later work.

items.title: Jimmy Owens interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: And within about two weeks I did a job with Slide Hampton. We went down to North Carolina and played a concert.

ctx.x: Brass players who had troubles, they would go to him. Well I studied with Carmine for a year and a half. I studied with the very eminent American composer Henry Brant. And I was learning my skills and I was saving my money to go to, at that time I really wanted to go to Juilliard because a lot of my friends had gone to Manhattan and they didn’t seem to like it. So I said I would go to Juilliard. I still had ambitions of playing European classical music. But still I was a jazz musician first. I worked the job for…
